name: Colombia
card_headline: De la Espriella ended total peace and launched a military offensive; clashes and drone attacks have risen as a December vote on a fiscal rescue bill nears.
card_summary: Abelardo de la Espriella, a Trump-backed outsider, won the June runoff 49.7 to 48.7 percent and took office on 7 August. [1][2] He ended Gustavo Petro's talks with armed groups in September and ordered an offensive. [3] Crisis Group counts about 27,000 members of armed and criminal groups. [4] Coca reached a record 261,000 hectares in 2024, and the deficit is near 7 percent of GDP. [5][6]
card_local: El Pais and Vanguardia report Indepaz's count of 45 social leaders and 26 massacres in the government's first 100 days, and Pares reports a rise in armed-group homicides since August. [7][8][9]
card_international: AP and Reuters covered the inauguration in Cali, and Al Jazeera, with AP, reported a drone attack that killed three soldiers on 8 November. [2][10][11]
card_scholar: Crisis Group and ACLED find armed-group numbers near 27,000 and the deadliest month of state-armed group clashes since 2018 in August. [4][12]
context_md: Colombia's 2016 peace accord with the FARC left other armed groups in place, and Pares reports that the ELN and the Gaitanist Army (the Clan del Golfo) expanded their reach afterwards. [13] Petro's government opened nine dialogue tables with about 14 groups under its total peace policy, and Crisis Group says a May poll found 62 percent of Colombians called it a failure. [4] Armed and criminal group membership rose from about 15,100 in 2022 to roughly 27,000 to 29,000 in 2025 and 2026, depending on who counts. [4][14] Abelardo de la Espriella, who had never held public office, won the 21 June runoff and was sworn in on 7 August in Cali. [2] The US sanctioned Petro in October 2025 and Trump endorsed De la Espriella before the vote. [15][16] A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck on 10 August, three days after the inauguration. [17]

sections.title: A one-point win, no majority in Congress, and a government run from the presidency
sections.body_md:
Abelardo de la Espriella, a lawyer and businessman, won the 21 June runoff over the leftist senator Ivan Cepeda by 49.7 percent to 48.7 percent in the initial count. Turnout was about 26.3 million of 41.4 million eligible voters. [1] The first round on 31 May gave him 44 percent to Cepeda's 41, according to the Congressional Research Service. Reuters' early count had 43 to 40. [18][19] Trump gave him a full endorsement on 2 June. [16]

Petro claimed fraud, which international observers and Colombian electoral authorities rejected, according to AP. Petro did not attend the inauguration in Cali on 7 August. [2] Reuters reported the next day that he had not recognised the result. [10] Cepeda conceded after a recount. [18]

The new president has no majority of his own. After the 8 March legislative elections the Historic Pact holds 25 of 103 Senate seats and 43 of 183 House seats, and Democratic Center holds 17 and 28. Parties with 61 percent of the Senate and 67 percent of the House joined his coalition, but in July the Historic Pact and Democratic Center together defeated his candidate for Senate president. [18]

La Silla Vacia's map of power, published 11 November, says the president acts as his own defence minister and that Ecopetrol is led by two friends of his who had no hydrocarbon experience. [20] El Pais counted at least nine early exits of ministers and agency heads in the first 100 days. It says the government formed a legislative majority quickly, that the submission law passed, and that the 2027 budget was issued by decree. [21]

lenses.local: La Silla Vacia and El Pais describe a government that built a working majority in Congress but has lost officials early and faces conflict-of-interest questions over appointments. [20][21]
lenses.international: AP and Reuters noted that the swearing-in took place in Cali, not at Congress in Bogota, and that Petro stayed away. [2][10]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie argues that the US can influence Latin American elections but its transactional approach cannot build lasting influence. [16]

sections.title: Total peace is closed and an offensive is on, with violence rising on every count
sections.body_md:
On 4 September De la Espriella announced the end of the talks his predecessor opened. The presidency then revoked the negotiators' appointments by Resolutions 390 and 391. The ELN table, installed in Caracas in November 2022, had been frozen by the ELN since February 2024. A legal-submission space with the Gaitanist Army (EGC, the Clan del Golfo) had been authorised in July 2024. [3] On 4 November Congress passed a bill that toughens terms for surrender: fighters must hand over weapons, assets, recruited minors and information on political ties to earn a lower sentence, and leaders face at least 10 years. [22][21]

How large the armed world is depends on who counts. Crisis Group puts members of armed and criminal groups at about 27,000, up from 15,132 in 2022, with armed members rising from 7,620 to 13,794. [4] The Ideas for Peace Foundation (FIP) counts about 29,000 in July 2026, up from 15,120 at the start of the Petro government. [14] FIP's 2025 figures, relayed by El Espectador, show the Clan del Golfo at 9,840 members, the ELN at 6,810, and the dissident factions led by Ivan Mordisco and Calarca at 4,019 and 2,958. [23] Pares argues the expansion began under President Juan Manuel Santos, not Petro. [13]

ACLED recorded at least 84 deaths in clashes between security forces and armed groups from 7 August to early September, making August the deadliest month for such clashes in its Colombia data since 2018. Air strikes between 27 and 31 August killed at least 31 fighters from two dissident factions. ACLED counted 30 drone attacks on security forces in the first three weeks. [12] The president promised to take down ten high-value targets in 90 days. El Pais reports a list of 43 names and three eliminated. [21] On 8 November a drone attack on an army base in Santa Rosa del Sur killed three soldiers and wounded at least 16. No group has been officially blamed. [11]

A Pares column dated 25 November, using Defence Ministry data for 7 August to 5 November, finds homicides attributed to armed groups at 515 against 124 in 2022, and confined people at 21,482 against 8,436. It says it is too early to tell whether this is a passing reaction or a lasting escalation. [9]

lenses.local: Pares and El Pais report rising homicides, confinement and attacks since August, and El Pais notes that the main ELN and dissident leaders have not been captured. [9][21] The Clan del Golfo told the president-elect that surrender is inevitable and the question is its terms. [24]
lenses.international: AP and Al Jazeera report drone attacks on soldiers, and Al Jazeera, citing wire services, reports the president's pledge to end negotiated peace. [11][25]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group recommends selective force, a bigger rural police presence and a legal framework that keeps dialogue possible. ACLED warns that using casualties as the measure of success could invite abuses against civilians. [4][12]

sections.title: Catatumbo: nearly two years of ELN against Frente 33, now fought with drones
sections.body_md:
The border region has been at war since January 2025, when the ELN and the Frente 33 dissidents began fighting over coca, laboratories and routes to Venezuela. El Pais calls it the main cocaine route to Venezuela, contested by at least 17 armed groups. Petro decreed a state of internal commotion on 24 January 2025, and a former FARC commander quoted by El Pais said it had no effect on territorial control. [26]

A command-post tally cut on 14 April 2026 recorded 173 homicides and more than 101,883 displaced people, according to Pares. The same Pares piece counts at least 200 drone attacks since January 2025 (a figure from the group Vivamos Humanos), says 49 minors were removed from armed groups in Catatumbo by the child welfare institute ICBF, and reports violence spreading to the Cucuta area, El Zulia and Villa del Rosario. [27]

Drones are now the main weapon. Corporeddeh counted 18 explosive drone attacks in 2026 up to 1 August, mostly in Tibu and El Tarra. They injured or killed 39 people, five of them soldiers or police killed and two civilians killed. The count excludes armed group losses. [28] Noticias RCN reported at least 25 drone attacks in the week to 26 October, with families leaving San Calixto and El Tarra and three people held hostage. [29]

The prize is coca. Norte de Santander had 48,739 hectares in 2024, mostly around Tibu. [30] On 30 October Venezuelan drones hit an ELN camp in Apure state, near the border, killing at least 19 people, among them Venezuelans, Colombians and Mexicans. The New York Times reported US assistance. Neither government has commented officially, InSight Crime says. [31] NTN24 reported on 9 November a Colombian bombing of ELN positions in Catatumbo, quoting the president, without casualty figures. [32]

lenses.local: El Pais, Vanguardia and Noticias RCN document drone attacks, displacement and confinement in Tibu, El Tarra and San Calixto. [28][29][26]
lenses.international: InSight Crime reports the first major Venezuelan strike on the ELN, after the US capture of Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and the installation of Delcy Rodriguez as interim president. [31]
lenses.scholar: Pares supplies the most detailed casualty and displacement tally, drawn from the official command post and civil society counts. [27]

sections.title: Record coca, suspended spraying and a decertification with a waiver
sections.body_md:
UNODC's survey, reported by El Pais, put coca at 261,000 hectares in 2024, up 3.5 percent from about 253,000 in 2023, with growth every year since about 204,000 hectares in 2021. [5] The 2023 survey had found potential cocaine production up 53 percent to 2,664 tonnes. [33] InSight Crime says 47 percent of the crop sits in 10 municipalities in four departments: Narino with 74,547 hectares (31,300 in Tumaco), Norte de Santander with 48,739, Putumayo with 44,473 and Cauca with 36,876. [30]

El Pais cites several causes. Manual eradication fell from more than 130,000 hectares in 2020 to 8,051 in 2025. A Constitutional Court ruling keeps aerial glyphosate spraying suspended. Armed groups control territory with little state presence, and the analyst Nestor Rosania says no other rural activity pays as well. Seizures were 395 tonnes from January to May 2026, 7 percent below the same months of 2025. [5]

De la Espriella plans to restart eradication with drones and bioherbicides and faces court requirements, approvals from the National Narcotics Council and environmental licences, InSight Crime reports. [30] Reuters reported he plans aerial herbicides. [10] He says he signed 41 extradition orders in his first 19 days. Rio Times reported no confirmed transfer as of 2 September. [34]

On 16 September the US kept Colombia on its list of countries that failed demonstrably on counternarcotics, but granted a national-interest waiver. The waiver gives Colombia 12 months to show results, and the White House said it would consider lifting the rating if coca eradication and the dismantling of networks advance. [35] Trump blamed Petro's policies for the rating, La Silla Vacia reported. [36]

lenses.local: El Pais and La Silla Vacia track the coca numbers and the decertification, and La Silla reports Trump blamed Petro, not the new government. [5][36]
lenses.international: Bloomberg Linea reports the waiver and the 12-month window to show results. [35]
lenses.scholar: UNODC's survey and InSight Crime's department-level breakdown are the main evidence on scale and concentration. [33][30]

sections.title: Washington backs the president, keeps the decertification and offers troops he may not be able to approve
sections.body_md:
Trump endorsed De la Espriella on 2 June. The US Treasury had already sanctioned Petro, his wife Veronica Alcocer, his son Nicolas Petro and then interior minister Armando Benedetti on 24 October 2025 under an executive order on the illicit drug trade. [16][15] Rio Times reported on 4 October that a Colombian outlet claimed the FBI could arrive and more sanctions were under review. No US agency had confirmed it. [15]

Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited on 8 September and signed memoranda on civil nuclear cooperation and critical minerals. He announced no new security assistance. On 7 August the administration said it would work with Congress on $1 billion in support. The FY2027 budget request includes at least $87 million for Colombia, and about $52 million in military financing was reportedly reprogrammed partly to Colombia. Congress had earlier cut Colombian aid and added conditions, and no reduction of US tariffs on Colombian goods has been announced. [18]

De la Espriella joined the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and the Shield of the Americas, and offered to host joint operations. Joint military operations could need Senate approval. [18] On 18 November La Silla Vacia relayed a New York Times report that he rejected a US offer from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to widen cooperation through joint operations, because officials say he lacks the Senate votes to authorise foreign troops. This rests on one report relayed second-hand. [37]

Venezuela is now part of the picture. After US forces captured Maduro in January 2026, Delcy Rodriguez governs as interim president under US pressure. Rubio said in September that Washington had discussed operations against the ELN in Venezuela with her administration. [31] Venezuela was not on the US decertification list. [36]

lenses.local: La Silla Vacia reports the decertification, the unconfirmed Hegseth offer and the limits on foreign troops in Colombia. [36][37]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, citing AFP, AP and Reuters, reported the $1 billion plan pending US Congress approval. [25] Bloomberg Linea reported the waiver. [35]
lenses.scholar: The Congressional Research Service lays out the aid, tariff and certification record, and Carnegie says Trump can pick winners but struggles to build lasting influence. [18][16]

sections.title: A deficit near 7 percent and a rescue law facing its first vote in December
sections.body_md:
Finance Minister Miguel Gomez put the fiscal deficit at 7 to 8 percent of GDP at the inauguration, above the outgoing government's figures. [10] bne IntelliNews gives the outgoing official figure as about 5.5 percent. [17] BBVA Research estimated on 23 October that the 2026 deficit will be 7.4 percent against a 7.2 percent target. It says the approved 2027 budget of COP 635 trillion implies 9.4 percent, that the government targets about 7.4 percent after its rescue bill, and that BBVA expects about 8 percent. Interest payments reached 27.5 percent of tax revenue by July. [6] El Pais puts public debt near 60 percent of GDP. [21]

The rescue law is a fiscal adjustment package inside a tax reform. The president said while marking his first 100 days that VAT on food would be dropped. Finance Minister Gomez projects a first-debate vote on 1 or 2 December. Senate president Honorio Henriquez said support would not be a blank check, and Democratic Center backs the aim but opposes measures that hit the family basket or rural producers. [38] After the changes, La Silla Vacia's calculator puts the government 15.6 trillion pesos short of an 80.6 trillion target, and corporate income tax stays at 35 percent. [37]

Petro and the Historic Pact kept a call for a national strike on 19 November against the tax bill and possible privatisation of Ecopetrol, Cenit and Grupo Bicentenario. The CUT union rejects those privatisations. [37] The government backs more oil and gas exploration, including what Reuters calls responsible fracking, and a stronger Ecopetrol. [10] The earthquake adds spending needs that bne IntelliNews says will test the austerity plan. [17]

lenses.local: El Pais and La Silla Vacia follow the rescue law's changes and the congressional bargaining over VAT and rural taxes. [38][37]
lenses.international: Reuters reported that investors welcomed the market-friendly agenda but that high public debt limits how fast change can come. [10]
lenses.scholar: BBVA Research expects the 2027 deficit near 8 percent, above the government's 7.4 percent target. [6]

sections.title: Leaders, signatories and journalists are still being killed under the new government
sections.body_md:
Indepaz counted 45 social leaders and human rights defenders killed between 7 August and 15 November, about one every 2.2 days. It also counted 8 signatories of the 2016 peace accord and 26 massacres with 87 victims, five of them minors. [7] Cauca had 11 leader killings, Antioquia 8 and Putumayo 4. In 44 of the 45 cases the perpetrator has not been identified, and 6,667 people were displaced in August and September. [8] Massacres were most frequent in Valle del Cauca (6), Antioquia (3) and Tolima (3). [7]

The Inter American Press Association said on 25 October that four journalists have been killed in Colombia in 2026. They are Mateo Perez Rueda (May, Antioquia), Cristian Herrera (June, Cucuta), Jader Durango (Cordoba) and Julian Hincapie, found on 2 October in Anori. Motives in the last two cases are unknown. [39] CPJ reported that Herrera, a board member of the press freedom group FLIP, was shot on 6 June outside his home. He had received at least 17 death threats since 2014. His assigned escorts were not with him at his own request, according to the protection unit. [40]

The new government plans to review Colombia's relationship with some international human rights mechanisms, according to Razon Publica. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace is investigating more than 6,000 alleged extrajudicial killings from 2002 to 2008. [41] Crisis Group warns that dismantling bodies such as the JEP could create legal chaos, and cites a UN count of about 493 former FARC members killed since 2016. [4]

lenses.local: El Pais and Vanguardia carry Indepaz's tallies, and Vanguardia reports the SIP's count of four journalists killed. [7][8][39]
lenses.international: CPJ's Latin America program coordinator said the government is not giving journalists even the most basic security measures, and CPJ called for prosecution of the killers of Perez Rueda. [40]
lenses.scholar: Razon Publica's Jose Luis Cotes argues that the key question is the rules, controls and accountability that govern force, citing the JEP's cases of killings presented as combat deaths. [41]

sections.title: An earthquake on top of a war, and 848,000 Venezuelans exposed to deportation
sections.body_md:
A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar in Choco on 10 August. [17] The Pan American Health Organization's sixth situation report, using figures from the national disaster agency UNGRD as of 25 August, counted 331 dead, 4,439 injured, 240 missing and 361,707 people affected across 16 departments. [42] The Norwegian Refugee Council reported 74,873 houses damaged and 12,584 destroyed by mid-August. It said more than nine million people in Colombia already relied on aid before the quake, and that in El Cairo, Valle del Cauca, 2,511 of 6,179 residents are registered conflict victims. [43] El Pais says aid reached Cali and Pereira slowly. [21]

On 23 August the president ordered Migracion Colombia and the police to find and deport migrants without legal status, starting with foreigners allegedly linked to crime. WOLA, using Migracion Colombia data through June 2026, counts about 2.8 million Venezuelans in Colombia, 527,525 of them irregular and 320,369 awaiting a temporary protection permit. If applied broadly, about 848,000 could be exposed. WOLA says conditions in Venezuela are unsafe after June 2026 earthquakes and continuing repression. [44]

lenses.local: El Pais reports slow earthquake aid to Cali and Pereira. [21]
lenses.international: bne IntelliNews reported the early toll and the president's emergency response, including a state of national disaster. [17]
lenses.scholar: PAHO, NRC and WOLA supply the casualty, housing and migrant figures. [42][43][44]

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters and AFP covered the election, the inauguration and the earthquake, and Al Jazeera and AP reported the November drone attack, but wire copy on Catatumbo and the daily killings of leaders is thin. [2][11][10] Colombian outlets, Pares, Indepaz, Crisis Group, ACLED and WOLA publish steadily. [7][4][12][44]

severity.basis: ACLED counts at least 84 deaths in state-armed group clashes in the first month of the new government, and membership of armed groups is about 27,000. [12][4]
A command-post tally records more than 101,883 displaced in Catatumbo, the earthquake left 331 dead and 361,707 affected, and more than nine million people relied on aid before it. [27][42][43]

Indepaz counts 45 social leaders killed in 100 days, SIP counts four journalists killed in 2026, and the presidential election was decided by one point and disputed by the outgoing president. [7][39][2]
The 2026 deficit is estimated at 7.4 percent of GDP, interest takes 27.5 percent of tax revenue, and the 2027 budget implies a 9.4 percent deficit. [6]
The government ended negotiations, violence indicators rose after 7 August, and coca reached a record in 2024. [3][9][5]

parts.basis: The US sanctioned Petro, endorsed his successor, kept Colombia decertified with a waiver, signed minerals and nuclear memoranda and pledged to seek $1 billion in support. [15][16][35][18]
Coca reached 261,000 hectares in 2024 and potential cocaine output was 2,664 tonnes in 2023, and oil and gas expansion with Ecopetrol is central to the government's plan. [5][33][10]
The ELN and dissidents operate across the Venezuelan border, where Venezuelan drones struck an ELN camp on 30 October, and the US reported discussions on operations there. [31]
Colombia hosts about 2.8 million Venezuelans, and about 848,000 could face deportation under the August order. [44]
A government has ended negotiated settlements with armed groups in favour of surrender or force, and the US sanctioned a sitting president over drug-trade allegations. [3][15]

summary: Colombia matters beyond its borders through cocaine supply, the Venezuelan border and the US alliance, and the US has stakes in each. [5][31][18]
The new government's switch from negotiation to force is a test case for other countries that have tried talks with armed groups, and Crisis Group warns it risks civilian harm. [4]
gi.up: A confirmed US-Colombian joint military operation, a Venezuelan crisis spilling across the border, or a large new migrant outflow.
gi.down: A held ceasefire with the ELN or the Clan del Golfo, a falling coca count, or a calmer border.

gaps: Cambio's pages could not be fetched (access refused) and Verdad Abierta returned no results, so neither is cited; local sourcing relies on El Pais Cali, Vanguardia, El Espectador, La Silla Vacia, Noticias RCN, El Heraldo and Razon Publica.
Indepaz's own reports were not opened; its counts reach this page through El Pais and Vanguardia.
RTVC and other state-run Colombian outlets were not read. Defence Ministry, UNGRD and Migracion Colombia figures appear only as relayed by Pares, PAHO and WOLA.
Armed-group totals differ between Crisis Group (about 27,000) and FIP (about 29,000), and first-round shares differ between Reuters (43 to 40) and CRS (44 to 41).

The Venezuelan strike on the ELN rests on InSight Crime, which relays a New York Times report on US help; the Hegseth offer rests on a La Silla Vacia roundup relaying the same newspaper. Neither is confirmed by an official source.
The Catatumbo displacement figure (more than 101,883) is a command-post tally relayed by Pares and sits well above the 64,000 Ombudsman figure for early 2025 reported by El Pais; the periods differ.
The outcome of the 19 November strike and the progress of the rescue bill after 18 November were not found.
No peer-reviewed academic study was read for this draft; scholar lens relies on Crisis Group, ACLED, Pares, WOLA, Carnegie, BBVA and Razon Publica.

The NTN24 report of a 9 November bombing in Catatumbo has no operational detail, and the 30 August killing of a dissident commander rests on the president's statement. The US boat strikes and the status of Petro after leaving office were not researched.
Podcast and documentary links point to listing pages; the Crisis Group episode page does not show a runtime.

reporters.why: His piece gives the clearest event-data picture of how violence changed after 7 August.

reporters.bio: Co-wrote the 8 July 2026 InSight Crime article with Sara Garcia on the new president's hard-line approach to coca.

reporters.label: InSight Crime

reporters.name: Johana Fiallo
reporters.bio: Wrote the 15 November 2026 El Pais report on Indepaz's tally for the government's first 100 days.
reporters.why: Her report gives department-level counts of social leaders and massacres.

reporters.name: Edgar Quintero Herrera
reporters.bio: Wrote the 11 November 2026 La Silla Vacia piece mapping who holds power in the De la Espriella government.

reporters.label: La Silla Vacia

reporters.name: Cindy A. Morales Castillo
reporters.bio: Wrote the 31 January 2026 El Espectador report on growth in armed-group membership, group by group.

reporters.name: Leon Valencia

factchecks.claim: Total peace caused armed groups to double in size.
factchecks.by: Argument in the debate over total peace, which a May poll found 62 percent of Colombians call a failure (Crisis Group).
factchecks.evidence: Crisis Group and FIP both find membership nearly doubled between 2022 and 2025 or 2026, but their totals differ (about 27,000 and about 29,000). Pares attributes the expansion to dynamics that began under Santos, and an Externado academic quoted by El Heraldo calls the policy overambitious for the state's capacity. FIP says ceasefires and suspended bombings helped groups expand.

factchecks.claim: The 2026 presidential election result was fraudulent.
factchecks.evidence: AP reports that international observers and Colombian electoral authorities rejected the fraud claim. Cepeda conceded after a recount, according to the Congressional Research Service. Carnegie describes Petro's separate claim of Israeli cyber interference as unsubstantiated. The margin was under one point, and Cepeda's campaign had challenged results at about 33,000 of 122,000 polling stations.

factchecks.claim: The United States has promised Colombia $1 billion in security assistance.
factchecks.by: US administration announcement of 7 August, as reported in wire coverage of the inauguration
factchecks.evidence: The Congressional Research Service says the administration announced it would work with Congress on $1 billion in support. The FY2027 request includes at least $87 million for Colombia, Rubio announced no new security assistance on 8 September, and the administration has not publicly released Colombia aid allocations since FY2024.

local_md:
La Silla Vacia and El Pais describe a government that built a working majority in Congress but has lost officials early and faces conflict-of-interest questions over appointments. [20][21]

Pares and El Pais report rising homicides, confinement and attacks since August, and El Pais notes that the main ELN and dissident leaders have not been captured. [9][21] The Clan del Golfo told the president-elect that surrender is inevitable and the question is its terms. [24]

El Pais, Vanguardia and Noticias RCN document drone attacks, displacement and confinement in Tibu, El Tarra and San Calixto. [28][29][26]

El Pais and La Silla Vacia track the coca numbers and the decertification, and La Silla reports Trump blamed Petro, not the new government. [5][36]

La Silla Vacia reports the decertification, the unconfirmed Hegseth offer and the limits on foreign troops in Colombia. [36][37]

El Pais and La Silla Vacia follow the rescue law's changes and the congressional bargaining over VAT and rural taxes. [38][37]

El Pais and Vanguardia carry Indepaz's tallies, and Vanguardia reports the SIP's count of four journalists killed. [7][8][39]

El Pais reports slow earthquake aid to Cali and Pereira. [21]
international_md:
AP and Reuters noted that the swearing-in took place in Cali, not at Congress in Bogota, and that Petro stayed away. [2][10]

AP and Al Jazeera report drone attacks on soldiers, and Al Jazeera, citing wire services, reports the president's pledge to end negotiated peace. [11][25]

InSight Crime reports the first major Venezuelan strike on the ELN, after the US capture of Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and the installation of Delcy Rodriguez as interim president. [31]

Bloomberg Linea reports the waiver and the 12-month window to show results. [35]

Al Jazeera, citing AFP, AP and Reuters, reported the $1 billion plan pending US Congress approval. [25] Bloomberg Linea reported the waiver. [35]

Reuters reported that investors welcomed the market-friendly agenda but that high public debt limits how fast change can come. [10]

CPJ's Latin America program coordinator said the government is not giving journalists even the most basic security measures, and CPJ called for prosecution of the killers of Perez Rueda. [40]

bne IntelliNews reported the early toll and the president's emergency response, including a state of national disaster. [17]
scholar_md:
Carnegie argues that the US can influence Latin American elections but its transactional approach cannot build lasting influence. [16]

Crisis Group recommends selective force, a bigger rural police presence and a legal framework that keeps dialogue possible. ACLED warns that using casualties as the measure of success could invite abuses against civilians. [4][12]

Pares supplies the most detailed casualty and displacement tally, drawn from the official command post and civil society counts. [27]

UNODC's survey and InSight Crime's department-level breakdown are the main evidence on scale and concentration. [33][30]

The Congressional Research Service lays out the aid, tariff and certification record, and Carnegie says Trump can pick winners but struggles to build lasting influence. [18][16]

BBVA Research expects the 2027 deficit near 8 percent, above the government's 7.4 percent target. [6]

Razon Publica's Jose Luis Cotes argues that the key question is the rules, controls and accountability that govern force, citing the JEP's cases of killings presented as combat deaths. [41]

PAHO, NRC and WOLA supply the casualty, housing and migrant figures. [42][43][44]
